title: China Southwest Airlines 4146
summary: China Southwest Airlines Flight 4146 was a domestic scheduled flight from Beijing to Chongqing with 98 passengers and 10 crew members. The flight was uneventful until 21:50 when near Chongqing, the aircraft's number four engine (outer right wing) caught fire. The fire burned through the engine mount causing the engine to fall off the aircraft's wing, resulting in loss of control. The aircraft hit a power line and two farmhouses before bursting into flames, killing all 108 occupants.
probable_cause: The crash of Flight 4146 was blamed on poor maintenance. The engine fire resulted from an oil leak caused by an overheated starter/generator that burned the oil supply tube when the propeller was feathered.

title: Avianca 410
summary: The aircraft took off from Cúcuta at 13:17 on runway 33 bound for Cartagena. Ground witnesses reported seeing the aircraft flying too low shortly after takeoff. The aircraft struck trees and then impacted a mountain head-on at 6,343 feet. The aircraft broke in half and disintegrated when the fuel exploded, with remains scattered in a 60 meter radius. The investigation determined that a non-crew pilot in the cockpit diverted the attention of the flying pilot and interfered with aircraft operation, combined with a lack of teamwork between pilot and copilot.
probable_cause: Controlled flight into terrain at 6,343 feet. The investigation pointed to a non-crew pilot in the cockpit whose presence diverted the attention of the pilot and interfered with the operation of the aircraft, and a lack of teamwork (crew resource management) between the pilot and copilot.

title: Widerøe 710

aircraft.type: de Havilland Canada DHC-7 Dash 7 Series 102

summary: Widerøe Flight 710 descended from 500 feet at eight nautical miles from Brønnøysund Airport instead of four nautical miles, striking Torghatten Mountain. The crew's situational awareness was degraded by inadequate communication, non-compliance with sterile cockpit procedures during approach with a passenger in the jump seat, and insufficient training. The first officer had minimal experience on the aircraft type.
probable_cause: The aircraft was descended from an unsafe altitude due to poor cockpit coordination, lack of sterile cockpit compliance, and inadequate crew communication and monitoring of the descent and approach plan.

title: Iran Air 655 shootdown
summary: Iran Air Flight 655, an Airbus A300 flying from Tehran to Dubai via Bandar Abbas, was shot down over the Persian Gulf on 3 July 1988 by two missiles from the USS Vincennes, killing all 290 aboard. The Vincennes crew, inexperienced in actual conflict, misidentified the airliner as an Iranian F-14 fighter despite its civilian transponder code, and after repeated radio challenges went unanswered, treated it as hostile before firing.
probable_cause: According to the United States, the Vincennes crew misidentified Flight 655 as a hostile F-14 fighter after receiving no response to repeated radio challenges and fired in the belief the aircraft posed a threat; the Iranian government maintains the US recklessly shot down the aircraft in violation of international law.

factors.evidence: its crew was inexperienced in actual conflict, but had performed well in training scenarios

events.text: Flight 655 left Bandar Abbas at 10:17 Iran Standard Time, 27 minutes behind its scheduled departure.
Flight 655 proceeded on an ascending flight path towards Vincennes while transmitting the correct civilian transponder squawk code.
Vincennes issued ten challenges to the airliner, seven on the Military Air Distress frequency and three on the International Air Distress frequency, but received no response.
Vincennes crew misidentified the aircraft as an Iranian F-14 Tomcat fighter despite its civilian identification codes and assumed it hostile.
Vincennes fired two surface-to-air missiles that hit the Airbus A300, killing all 290 people on board.

title: Vietnam Airlines 831
summary: Vietnam Airlines Flight 831 crashed in a rice field 6 km north of Bangkok International Airport on 9 September 1988. The flight crew reported the aircraft may have been struck by lightning as it approached to land in heavy rain. The navigator shouted Lightning, it's lightning. However, no warnings were made, and they continued their descent. When the aircraft descended to 380 meters, light flashed, incapacitating the cabin crews. The aircraft descended below the minimum safe altitude and crashed into the ground.
probable_cause: Lightning strike during approach in heavy rain caused crew incapacitation at a critical moment, preventing control inputs needed to arrest descent.

title: Indian Airlines 113
summary: Boeing 737 crashed during localiser-DME approach to Ahmedabad in low visibility. Crew descended to 204 feet below 500-foot minimum descent altitude without sighting runway, struck trees and high-tension electrical transmission pylon. Both pilots focused on attempting to see runway rather than monitoring instruments, losing track of altitude.
probable_cause: Pilot error and non-adherence to procedures with both pilots focused on seeing the runway instead of monitoring altimeter, combined with poor visibility and absence of approach lights and glide path.

title: 1988 Soviet Air Force Il-76 crash
summary: A Soviet Air Force Il-76M aircraft crashed into a mountainside during descent to Leninakan, Armenia while participating in relief efforts following the Spitak earthquake. The crash was caused by incorrect altimeter setting by the flight crew, which gave an altitude reading 1,100 meters higher than actual altitude. Crew fatigue from multiple relief flights the previous day also contributed.
probable_cause: The crash was eventually attributed to an incorrect altimeter setting by the flight crew which gave an incorrect altitude reading that was 1,100 m higher than the actual altitude. Crew fatigue was also cited as a factor in the crash as the flight crew was not given enough rest after carrying out multiple relief flights the previous day.

title: Pan Am 103
summary: Pan Am Flight 103, a Boeing 747 flying from Frankfurt to Detroit via London and New York, was destroyed by a bomb while cruising over Lockerbie, Scotland, on 21 December 1988, killing all 259 aboard and 11 people on the ground. Investigators found the explosion tore a hole in the fuselage, the nose was blown off within seconds, and disrupted elevator and rudder cables caused the aircraft to break apart; Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was convicted of the bombing in 2001.
probable_cause: Investigators concluded a bomb concealed in the cargo hold exploded in flight, tearing open the fuselage and severing flight control cables, causing the aircraft to break up over Lockerbie; Libyan intelligence officer Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was convicted of 270 counts of murder for the bombing in 2001.

factors.evidence: The Boeing 747 Clipper Maid of the Seas was destroyed by a bomb while flying over the Scottish town of Lockerbie; in 2001 Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was found guilty of 270 counts of murder in connection with the bombing.
The explosion tore a 50 cm hole in the left side of the fuselage, causing the upper deck walls and roof to rip away from the plane within the first few seconds post-explosion.
The aircraft's elevator- and rudder-control cables were disrupted and the fuselage pitched downwards and to the left.
The nose of the aircraft was blown off and separated from the main fuselage within three seconds of the explosion, striking the number-three engine before the wreckage fell near Lockerbie.

events.text: Shortly after 19:00 GMT on 21 December 1988 the Boeing 747 Clipper Maid of the Seas was destroyed by a bomb while flying over the Scottish town of Lockerbie.
The explosion tore a 50 cm hole in the left side of the fuselage, ripping the upper deck walls and roof away within the first few seconds.
No distress call was recorded; a 180-millisecond hissing noise was captured on the cockpit voice recorder as the explosion destroyed the aircraft's communications center.
Within three seconds the nose of the aircraft was blown off and separated from the fuselage, briefly held on by a band of metal before shearing off and striking the number-three engine.

The elevator- and rudder-control cables were disrupted and the fuselage pitched downwards and to the left as the aircraft broke apart and fell near Lockerbie, killing all 259 aboard and 11 on the ground.
